The dots are blinking independently, randomly, every frame! This is a display effect — the dots are flickering (like a "twinkling" animation), and the segmentation is randomly detecting them. So the dots are always at fixed positions: (3,15), (9,6), (9,24), (17,15) — they never actually move or get collected!
Wait, but earlier I thought (17,15) was "collected" — the frame was split and the child disappeared. But that was just the dot being in the "off" phase of the blink, plus the arm covering the frame. And the "collection" of (9,24) in the previous turn — that was also just a blink.
So nothing has been collected! The dots are just blinking (a visual effect, probably to make them stand out). The frames are fixed 3×3 charcoal squares, and the dots blink in and out.
Hmm, so what's the actual goal? Let me reconsider. The dots blink. The cross moves. SPACE switches the active cross. What is the win condition?
Maybe the goal is: to align the center of the cross with each dot's position (the center pixel of the frame) — i.e., "visit" all 4 yellow dots with the yellow cross (and all 4 blue dots with the blue cross)? And the blinking is just decoration.
Or maybe the goal is for the cross's arms to cover the dots? Or for the center to land exactly on a dot?
Evidence so far:
- Center landed on (3,15) (frame 26: W (3,15), Y has (17,15) but no (3,15) — the dot is hidden by the center). No level completion.
- Score is still 0, no level completion.
Hmm, so landing on a dot doesn't complete the level. Maybe the level only completes when all dots of the active color have been "collected," and collection requires the center to pass through while the dot is lit? That seems too random.
Let me think about the blinking pattern. Maybe the blinking is deterministic (e.g., each dot blinks with a period, or a global pattern). Let me tabulate the presence of each dot across frames 0–29:
(3,15): frames 0-5 present, 6 absent, 7-12 present, 13 absent, 14-18 present, 19 absent, 20-23 present, 24 absent, 25 absent, 26 present, 27 present, 28 absent, 29 present.

(9,6): 0-8 present, 9 absent, 10-15 present, 16 absent, 17-20 present, 21 present, 22-27 present, 28 absent, 29 absent.
(9,24): 0-8 present, 9 absent, 10-12 present, 13 absent, 14-18 present, 19 absent, 20-23 present, 24 absent, 25-27 present, 28 absent, 29 absent.
(17,15): 0-5 present, 6 absent, 7-8 present, 9-12 present, 13 absent, 14-18 present, 19 absent, 20 absent, 21 absent, 22-23 present, 24 absent, 25-27 present, 28 absent, 29 present.
Interesting: (9,24) is absent in frames 9, 13, 19, 24, 28. (9,6) is absent in 9, 16, 28, 29. (3,15) is absent in 6, 13, 19, 24, 28. (17,15) is absent in 6, 13, 19, 20, 21, 24, 28.

Maybe the blinking is a global "wave" — a diagonal or column-based wave that passes through and temporarily hides the dots. At frame 24 (all absent) and 28 (all absent) — the wave covers everything every 4 frames? But at frame 20: only (17,15) absent. Frame 21: (17,15) absent. Frame 22: (3,15),(17,15) absent. Frame 23: (3,15),(17,15) absent.
Hmm, this is messy. Maybe each dot blinks independently with a random period.
Key insight: the dots are probably just a blinking decoration, and the real goal is something else. Let me reconsider the whole game.
What do we know?
- Two crosses (yellow active, blue inactive), each with a white center pixel.
- SPACE switches the active cross (yellow ↔ blue).

- 4 yellow dots in frames near the yellow cross's home region (upper left), 4 blue dots in frames near the blue cross's home region (right).

Maybe the goal is: to move the yellow cross so that its center covers all 4 yellow dots in sequence (visits), and same for blue. "Visit" = center lands on the dot's cell. And the level completes when all 4+4 have been visited. The dots blink but stay in place.

Or "visit" might mean the center passes through (slides over) the dot's cell.
Or maybe the goal is to align the cross so that all 4 dots are simultaneously covered by the arms? The dots are at (3,15),(9,6),(9,24),(17,15). The cross's arms extend 11px from the center. Can a single cross position cover all 4 dots with its arms/center? The dots span rows 3-17, columns 6-24. The cross is a plus: horizontal arm (row c, columns c-11..c+11) and vertical arm (column c, rows c-11..c+11). To cover (3,15) and (17,15): the vertical arm needs to cover rows 3-17 in some column — if the center's column is 15, the vertical arm covers rows c-11..c+11; to cover 3 and 17: c-11<=3 and c+11>=17 → c<=14 and c>=6 → c in 6..14, and c≡0 mod 3: c=9 or 12. To cover (9,6) and (9,24): the horizontal arm needs to cover columns 6-24 in some row: c-11<=6 and c+11>=24 → c<=17 and c>=13 → c=15. But c can't be both 9/12 and 15. Collection probably happens when the center lands on a dot (or passes through it). Since nothing has been collected yet despite landing on (3,15)… hmm, that contradicts "landing collects."
Wait, let me actually re-verify: at frame 26, W=(3,15). Was the dot at (3,15) "on" at that moment? Frame 26's Y list: [(9,6),(9,24),(17,15)] — (3,15) is absent. But that's because the center is covering it (the white pixel overwrote it), or because it's in the off phase. Frame 25: (3,15) absent. Frame 27: (3,15) present. So (3,15) is blinking; the center was on top of it at frame 26.
If landing collected, then (3,15) should be permanently off from frame 26 onward. But it's on at frame 27 and 29. So landing doesn't collect. Confirmed.
So what does collect? Maybe passing through (sliding over) the dot's cell? At frame 26, the center slid (6,15)→(3,15), passing through (5,15),(4,15) — not (3,15) as an intermediate point. Then at frame 27 it slid (3,15)→(6,15), passing through (4,15),(5,15). So (3,15) was only an endpoint. Consistent with "passing through collects, landing doesn't."
But earlier I "confirmed" that (17,15) was collected by passing through (slide 15→18 passing through 16,17). But now I know the dots blink — the "collection" of (17,15) was just a blink-off phase! The frame split at (17,15) was just the arm covering it. So the pass-through theory is also unconfirmed.
Ugh. OK, so what we know for sure:
1. The dots blink (a visual effect). All 8 dots are still present.
2. Landing on a dot doesn't collect it (the dot at (3,15) is still blinking after the center landed on it).
3. Nothing has been collected yet. Score 0.
Let me look at the blinking pattern more carefully — maybe it's not random. Maybe the dots blink in a pattern that indicates something (like a sequence to follow?). Or maybe the blinking is tied to the timer.
Actually, let me step back and think about the game design. This looks like a "collect the dots" game with two vehicles. The dots blink to be visible against the black background. The purple bar is a countdown timer. Goal: collect all dots before the timer runs out. Collection mechanism: the cross's center overlaps the dot — but maybe collection requires the dot to be "on" at the moment of overlap? Or maybe collection happens when the center passes over the dot's cell during a move (a sweep), not when it's stationary?
Hmm, at frame 26 the center was stationary at (3,15) for 1 frame (the landing frame). Maybe collection requires the center to be on the dot at the end of a move, and the dot to be lit? At frame 26, the dot (3,15) was in the off phase (absent in frames 25 and 26). So maybe collection failed because the dot was off!
This is a plausible mechanic: the dots blink on/off, and you can only collect when the dot is lit. The blinking might be deterministic per dot (e.g., a period).
Let me analyze the blink periods. For each dot, list the frames where it's off (excluding frames where the center covers it):
Center positions per frame (W):
0:(45,36) 1:(42,36) 2:(27,21) 3:(27,18) 4:(24,18) 5:(21,18) 6:(18,18) 7:(15,18) 8:(15,21) 9:(15,24) 10:(12,24) 11:(12,21) 12:(12,18) 13:(12,15) 14:(12,12) 15:(12,9) 16:(12,6) 17:(12,9) 18:(12,12) 19:(12,15) 20:(15,15) 21:(18,15) 22:(15,15) 23:(12,15) 24:(9,15) 25:(6,15) 26:(3,15) 27:(6,15) 28:(9,15) 29:(9,12)
Dot (3,15) is off at: 6,13,19,24,25,28. The center covers (3,15) only at frame 26. So off: 6,13,19,24,25,28. Gaps: 6→13 (7), 13→19 (6), 19→24 (5), 25, 28. Hmm, not a clean period.
Dot (9,6) is off at: 9,16,28,29. Gaps: 7, 12, 1.
Dot (9,24) is off at: 9,13,19,24,28. Gaps: 4,6,5,4.
Dot (17,15) is off at: 6,13,19,20,21,24,28. Gaps: 7,6,1,1,4,4.
Not periodic. Looks random. So the blinking is random per frame (each dot has some probability of being off each frame).
Hmm, if collection requires the dot to be lit at the moment of overlap, and the blinking is random, then the strategy is: repeatedly land on the dot until it's lit. But how do you know if you collected? The dot stops blinking (permanently off).
Alternatively, maybe collection happens on pass-through (sweep) and the dot's state doesn't matter.
I need a discriminating experiment. Let me design one:
- Move the center to pass through a dot's cell as an intermediate point of a slide, and check if the dot stops blinking.
- Example: dot (9,24): slide the center from (9,21) to (9,24)? That's landing. From (9,27) to (9,24)? Landing. Wait. That's a critical realization. All 8 dots are at positions ≡ (0,0) mod 3 (check: (3,15)✓, (9,6)✓, (9,24)✓, (17,15)✗! 17 mod 3 = 2. (17,15): 17≡2, 15≡0. Not ≡(0,0)!)
Blue dots: (16,48): 16≡1. (24,40): 24≡0, 40≡1. (24,53): 53≡2. (35,48): 35≡2.

For a dot to be collected by pass-through (as an intermediate point of a slide), the dot must be at a ≡(1,0),(2,0),(0,1),(0,2) mod 3 position along the slide's axis… e.g., dot (17,15): column 15≡0, row 17≡2. Dot (9,6): (0,0) mod 3 — endpoint only.
Dot (9,24): (0,0) — endpoint only.
Blue (16,48): 16≡1, 48≡0 — a vertical slide in column 48 passes through it as an intermediate point ✓.

Blue (24,53): 53≡2 — a horizontal slide in row 24 ✓.

Hmm, but that's a weird mechanic. Let me reconsider: maybe collection requires the center to be on the dot at the end of a move, and the dot to be lit in the resulting frame.
Or maybe the blinking is unrelated to collection, and collection requires something else entirely — e.g., the dot must be covered by an arm (not the center)? Or the goal isn't collection at all.
Let me look at the image again. The dots are inside 3×3 charcoal frames. The frames look like "sockets." The cross's center is a white pixel. Maybe the goal is to "dock" the center into each socket (frame center = dot position). The blinking dots are just indicators.
Given the uncertainty, the best move is a discriminating experiment:

Currently lit yellow dots: (3,15) and (17,15) (frame 29). The center is at (9,12).

Oh. The center can never be at row 17 (≡2 mod 3). So (17,15) can only be collected by pass-through (a vertical slide in column 15 from 15→18 or 18→15… wait, the slide from 15 to 18 passes through 16,17 ✓).
So: (17,15) requires pass-through; (3,15),(9,6),(9,24) require landing (they're ≡(0,0)).
So the collection rule must be: the center's trajectory (including the landing point) covers the dot's cell. That is, if the dot's cell is anywhere along the slide (including the endpoint), it's collected. Then:
- (17,15): collected by the slide 15→18 (already done at frame 21!). But it's still blinking. So it wasn't collected. Hmm!

Unless the game checks the intermediate positions of the slide with the dot's state at the start of the move or something. This is getting too speculative.
Let me reconsider: maybe the blinking isn't random — maybe the dots blink in sync with something, and there's a deterministic window. Let me look at the off frames again:

Actually, a better experiment: (3,15) is lit now. Land on it: RIGHT×1, UP×5. Then observe (3,15) over the next few frames — if it's permanently off while the others blink, it's collected.
But wait — if the rule is "land while lit," then the dot's state at the landing frame matters, and the dot might blink off during the 6-move approach. I can't control that. But I can retry.
Alternatively, the rule might be "the center passes over the dot during a move, and the dot is lit at the start of the move." For (3,15): the move UP from (6,15) to (3,15) — the dot is at the endpoint.
Let me just do the experiment: RIGHT×1, UP×5 (land on (3,15)), then observe the dot's state in the next 2-3 frames (with a few neutral moves? no — neutral moves change the center; I can just observe the current frame over time… but the frame only updates on actions. Hmm, the blinking updates per action (per frame). So to observe the dot's state over time, I have to keep taking actions.
Plan:
1. RIGHT×1, UP×5 → land on (3,15).
2. Then DOWN×1, UP×1, DOWN×1, UP×1 (jitter around (3,15)/(6,15)) to generate frames and observe (3,15)'s blink state.

Let me execute step 1 and the observation jitter in one batch, and print the Y dots after each action. action() returns after the whole batch, but I can call action() multiple times in the same Python code and check the state in between!
Code:

sections.content:
**Major revision**: The dots are *blinking* — they randomly appear/disappear frame by frame, and all 8 are still present (nothing has been collected). The "collection" I thought I saw was just the blink-off phase. Key facts:
- The center is always ≡(0,0) mod 3, so it can *land* on (3,15), (9,6), (9,24), but can never land on (17,15) (row 17≡2) — that one can only be crossed during a slide.
- The center landed on (3,15) at frame 26 while the dot was in its off phase → no collection. The slide crossed (17,15) at frame 21 while that dot was off → no collection.
- **Hypothesis**: A dot is collected only when the center covers it at the end of a move *and the dot is lit at that moment*.
Experiment: (3,15) is currently lit. Land on it (RIGHT, UP×5), then jitter away and back to check whether it has permanently stopped blinking.

sections.content:
<tool_call>
<function=python>
<parameter=code>
def dots():
    seg = current_frame.segmentation
    y=[]
    for n in seg['nodes']:
        if n['pixels']<=2 and n['color']=='Y':
            b=n['boundary']; y.append((min(p[0] for p in b),min(p[1] for p in b)))
    ws=[(min(p[0] for p in n['boundary']),min(p[1] for p in n['boundary'])) for n in seg['nodes'] if n['color']=='W']
    return sorted(y), ws[0]
action(['RIGHT']); print("after RIGHT:", dots())
action(['UP']*5); print("after UPx5 (on 3,15):", dots())
action(['DOWN']); print("check1:", dots())
action(['UP']); print("back on:", dots())
action(['DOWN']); print("check2:", dots())
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

Controls: arrow keys + SPACE.
- Open questions: what does SPACE do; how are dots collected (center alignment? crossing a dot?).
- Plan: probe LEFT once to confirm step size on the yellow cross.

世界模型结束。

But earlier I "confirmed" that (17,15) was collected by passing through (slide 15→18 passing through 16,17). But now I know the dots blink — the "collection" of (17,15) was just a blink-off phase! Ugh. OK, so what we know for sure:

Actually, let me step back and think about the game design. This looks like a "collect the dots" game with two vehicles. The dots blink to be visible against the black background. The purple bar is a countdown timer. Goal: collect all dots before the timer runs out. Collection mechanism: the cross's center overlaps the dot — but maybe collection requires the dot to be "on" at the moment of overlap? sections.content:
**Major revision**: The dots are *blinking* — they randomly appear/disappear frame by frame, and all 8 are still present (nothing has been collected). The "collection" I thought I saw was just the blink-off phase. Key facts:
- The center is always ≡(0,0) mod 3, so it can *land* on (3,15), (9,6), (9,24), but can never land on (17,15) (row 17≡2) — that one can only be crossed during a slide.
- The center landed on (3,15) at frame 26 while the dot was in its off phase → no collection. The slide crossed (17,15) at frame 21 while that dot was off → no collection.
- **Hypothesis**: A dot is collected only when the center covers it at the end of a move *and the dot is lit at that moment*.
Experiment: (3,15) is currently lit. Land on it (RIGHT, UP×5), then jitter away and back to check whether it has permanently stopped blinking.

sections.label: TOOL CALL: python
sections.content:
<tool_call>
<function=python>
<parameter=code>
def dots():
    seg = current_frame.segmentation
    y=[]
    for n in seg['nodes']:
        if n['pixels']<=2 and n['color']=='Y':
            b=n['boundary']; y.append((min(p[0] for p in b),min(p[1] for p in b)))
    ws=[(min(p[0] for p in n['boundary']),min(p[1] for p in n['boundary'])) for n in seg['nodes'] if n['color']=='W']
    return sorted(y), ws[0]
action(['RIGHT']); print("after RIGHT:", dots())
action(['UP']*5); print("after UPx5 (on 3,15):", dots())
action(['DOWN']); print("check1:", dots())
action(['UP']); print("back on:", dots())
action(['DOWN']); print("check2:", dots())
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
